## Introduction

<!--
- 2-3 sentences: why survival analysis instead of plain classification for churn.
- Key idea: churn is time-to-event, not just yes/no. Classification throws away
  *when* a customer churns; survival analysis keeps it.
- State the business question, e.g.:
  "How long do customers stay before churning, and which factors accelerate
  or delay churn?"
-->

## Data

<!--
- Dataset: Telco Customer Churn (Kaggle) or your own.
- Required columns: tenure (duration), Churn (event indicator), covariates.
- Note censoring: customers still active at data collection = censored, not "no event".
-->

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(randomForestSRC)

df <- read_csv("data/WA_Fn-UseC_-Telco-Customer-Churn.csv")  # update path
glimpse(df)
```

```{r}
# Basic cleaning
# - TotalCharges is stored as character with 11 blank (" ") entries, all at
#   tenure = 0 (brand-new customers, never billed). These have no observed
#   survival time, so they're dropped rather than imputed.
# - Churn recoded to 0/1 event indicator.
# - customerID kept for reference but excluded from modeling formulas.
# - SeniorCitizen cast to factor (stored as 0/1 int, but categorical).

df <- df %>%
  filter(tenure > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    Churn = ifelse(Churn == "Yes", 1, 0),
    TotalCharges = as.numeric(TotalCharges),
    SeniorCitizen = factor(SeniorCitizen, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

summary(df)
```

### Censoring check

<!-- Show proportion censored vs event observed -- standard in a survival
     write-up, reviewers will look for it. -->

```{r}
event_rate <- mean(df$Churn)
cat(sprintf("Event (churn) rate: %.2f%%\n", event_rate * 100))
cat(sprintf("Censored rate: %.2f%%\n", (1 - event_rate) * 100))
```

## Exploratory Analysis

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(x = tenure, fill = factor(Churn))) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Tenure (months)", y = "Count", fill = "Churned") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Kaplan-Meier Estimation

<!--
- Overall survival curve.
- Segmented KM curves by a key categorical variable (e.g. Contract type).
- Log-rank test to confirm segments differ significantly.
-->

```{r}
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ 1, data = df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_fit,
  data = df,
  title = "Overall Survival Curve",
  xlab = "Tenure (months)",
  ylab = "Survival Probability"
)
```

```{r}
# Segmented by a key variable -- update column name if needed
km_fit_group <- survfit(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ Contract, data = df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_fit_group,
  data = df,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  title = "Survival Curves by Contract Type"
)
```

<!-- Interpretation: state p-value, whether survival differs significantly
     between groups, and what that means for the business. -->

## Cox Proportional Hazards Model

```{r}
# customerID excluded -- identifier, not a predictor
df_model <- df %>% select(-customerID)

cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ ., data = df_model)
summary(cox_fit)
```

<!-- Interpretation: pick 2-3 covariates with notable hazard ratios and explain
     in plain language, e.g. "Month-to-month contract customers have a hazard
     ratio of X relative to two-year contracts -- Xx more likely to churn at
     any given time." -->

### Proportional Hazards Assumption Check

<!--
This is the step most portfolio projects skip. Including it signals rigor.
-->

```{r}
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test
ggcoxzph(ph_test)
```

<!-- If the assumption is violated for a variable, note it -- e.g. stratify by
     that variable instead of including it as a linear covariate. Discuss
     briefly; don't need to fully resolve it for portfolio purposes, just
     show you checked and understand what a violation implies. -->

## Random Survival Forest (Flexible Alternative)

<!--
Motivation: Cox assumes a linear, additive log-hazard. RSF relaxes this,
capturing nonlinear effects and interactions without specifying a functional
form -- same "classical vs. flexible model" theme as the GARCH-RNN project.
-->

```{r}
rsf_fit <- rfsrc(
  Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ .,
  data = df_model,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rsf_fit)
```

### Variable Importance

```{r}
plot(gg_vimp(rsf_fit))
```

## Model Comparison

<!--
Primary metric: concordance index (C-index) -- standard in survival analysis,
NOT accuracy/AUC. Compare Cox PH vs RSF on held-out test set (or OOB for RSF).
-->

```{r}
# Cox concordance (from model summary, or recompute on held-out test set)
cox_c_index <- summary(cox_fit)$concordance["C"]

# RSF out-of-bag concordance
rsf_c_index <- 1 - rsf_fit$err.rate[length(rsf_fit$err.rate)]

cat(sprintf("Cox PH C-index: %.4f\n", cox_c_index))
cat(sprintf("RSF C-index: %.4f\n", rsf_c_index))
```

<!--
Discuss honestly:
- If RSF barely beats Cox, that's a valid finding (relationships are mostly
  linear/additive in this dataset) -- same honest-null framing as the
  "flat likelihood valley" conclusion in the GARCH-RNN project.
- If RSF clearly wins, point to which nonlinear interactions it likely
  captured that Cox couldn't (variable importance plot helps here).
-->
